structure.title: I
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway, Nick Carraway, reflecting on his father's advice to reserve judgment, which has made him a reluctant confidant to others but left him disillusioned after witnessing moral chaos in the East—except for Gatsby, whose extraordinary gift for hope he finds unmatched. In spring 1922, Nick moves alone to West Egg, renting a modest eighty-dollar-a-month bungalow between two grand estates, and buys twelve volumes on banking as symbols of his ambition to become a 'well-rounded man.' That evening, he drives by car to East Egg to dine with his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, whom he knew at Yale; during dinner, Tom delivers a racist tirade about 'The Rise of the Coloured Empires,' a telephone call reveals his affair in New York, and Daisy, in a moment of cynical despair, tells Nick she hopes her daughter will be a 'beautiful little fool.' Afterward, Nick returns home to West Egg, where he sees Gatsby standing alone in the shadows of his mansion, arms outstretched toward a single green light at the end of a distant dock, before Gatsby vanishes into the night.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer afternoon, Nick Carraway travels by train with Tom Buchanan from West Egg toward New York when the train halts in the desolate valley of ashes, forcing them to disembark and visit George Wilson’s dilapidated garage, where Tom introduces Nick to his mistress, Myrtle Wilson, who is visibly vibrant yet dismissive of her spiritless husband. The trio departs for New York via separate train cars, arriving at Myrtle’s apartment on 158th Street, where she buys a $10 Airedale puppy, changes into a cream-coloured chiffon dress, and transforms into an affected socialite; later, her sister Catherine and the McKees arrive, and during the drunken gathering, Myrtle repeatedly utters Daisy’s name, provoking Tom to violently break her nose, sparking chaos as women rush to assist and Mr. McKee silently witnesses the aftermath before leaving, leaving Nick exhausted and alone in the cold lower level of Pennsylvania Station, waiting for the four o’clock train.

structure.title: III
characters_present: The drunken man in the library
The driver of the crashed coupé
structure.summary: On a Saturday evening shortly after seven, Nick Carraway arrives by car at Jay Gatsby’s lavish mansion on Long Island, invited by a formal note, and finds a chaotic, opulent party in full swing with guests arriving by car and train, orchestras playing, caterers serving extravagant food, and servants repairing nightly damage. As he wanders among strangers, he overhears wild rumors about Gatsby—such as that he killed a man or was a German spy—and eventually meets Jordan Baker, who guides him through the party’s social layers, including an encounter with a drunken man in the Gothic library who confirms Gatsby’s books are real, and a WWI veteran who invites him to fly in a hydroplane the next morning. Later, Nick Carraway sits at a table with a man who reveals himself to be Gatsby, who extends the same hydroplane invitation, while Jordan informs him she doubts Gatsby’s claim of having attended Oxford; as the party descends into disorder—with a chorus girl weeping ink-black tears, guests arguing, and Owl Eyes and another man crashing Gatsby’s new coupé into a wall—Nick Carraway observes Gatsby standing alone, sober and composed, before seeing him gesture farewell on the porch under a pale moon as the noise fades. The chapter concludes with Nick Carraway reflecting on his daily life in New York: commuting on foot to the Probity Trust, dining with clerks, studying at the Yale Club library, and walking home past Madison Avenue and 33rd Street to Pennsylvania Station, where he observes the city’s vibrant nightlife; he recounts a brief romantic involvement with a girl from Jersey City that ended due to her brother’s disapproval and her July vacation, and his rekindled connection with Jordan Baker, whom he admires for her fame as a golf champion but later discovers to be dishonest after learning she lied about damaging a borrowed car and cheated in a major tournament, leading him to resolve to end his unresolved correspondence with a woman back home while declaring himself one of the few honest people he has ever known.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning in July 1922, Gatsby’s mansion hosts a chaotic, glittering party as guests arrive by car from East Egg, West Egg, and New York, including a long list of transient figures like Ripley Snell, Klipspringer, and Benny McClenahan, who gossip about Gatsby’s rumored criminal past without knowing him personally; later that month, Gatsby picks up Nick Carraway in his cream-colored car with a three-noted horn, drives him to town, and delivers an elaborate, nervously delivered fabricated backstory claiming Oxford education, European aristocracy, and wartime heroism—backed by a Montenegrin medal and an Oxford photograph—before revealing he needs Nick Carraway’s help to reconnect with Daisy Baker; at noon in a cellar on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfshiem, a grotesque underworld figure whose cuff buttons are made of human molars, who recounts the murder of Rosy Rosenthal and attempts to involve Nick Carraway in business, only for Gatsby to abruptly leave and later vanish from the restaurant after being introduced to Tom Buchanan; meanwhile, in flashbacks set in 1917, Jordan Baker recalls meeting Daisy Fay in Louisville as she sat in her white roadster with Lieutenant Jay Gatsby, later learning of Daisy’s troubled marriage to Tom Buchanan, including her drunken wedding-day meltdown over a $350,000 pearl necklace and Tom’s affair; finally, at twilight, Jordan reveals to Nick Carraway that Gatsby bought his mansion solely so Daisy could see the green light across the bay, and he has been cautiously seeking an introduction through Nick Carraway, not Jordan, fearing offense, prompting Nick Carraway to shift focus from Gatsby’s obsession to a quiet, intimate moment with Jordan as they ride through Central Park.

structure.title: V
structure.summary: On a rainy evening, Nick returns to West Egg to find Gatsby’s mansion brilliantly lit and eerily silent; Gatsby approaches him nervously, inviting him to Coney Island or a swim, then awkwardly proposes a side business, revealing his insecurity about Nick’s financial standing. The next day, Nick calls Daisy to invite her to tea, explicitly warning her not to bring Tom. As rain pours during the appointed hour, Gatsby sends a man to cut Nick’s grass and delivers a greenhouse full of flowers, arriving himself in a white flannel suit, silver shirt, and gold tie, visibly shaken and sleep-deprived. When Daisy arrives in a large open car, Gatsby freezes at the door, pale and trembling; their reunion is strained—Gatsby nearly knocks over a mantel clock—until, after Nick briefly leaves, they emerge transformed: Daisy tear-streaked, Gatsby glowing with quiet joy, now confidently inviting her to tour his mansion. As the rain clears, Gatsby leads Daisy through opulent rooms—including Marie Antoinette music-rooms and Restoration Salons—where they encounter Mr. Klipspringer in pajamas doing liver exercises. In Gatsby’s study, he displays piles of luxurious shirts in silk, linen, and flannel, adorned with stripes, scrolls, and monograms in coral, lavender, and Indian blue, causing Daisy to sob uncontrollably. Gatsby points out the green light on Daisy’s dock, acknowledging its diminished symbolic power; Nick examines photographs of Dan Cody and a youthful Gatsby in yachting attire, while Daisy playfully teases him about his pompadour. Gatsby shows newspaper clippings about Daisy and answers a frustrated phone call regarding Detroit being mistaken for a 'small town.' As pink and golden clouds appear, Daisy whimsically wishes to enclose Gatsby within one; Gatsby summons Klipspringer to play piano in the dimly lit music room, where he lights Daisy’s cigarette and sits with her in shadow. Nick departs alone into the rain, observing Gatsby’s return to bewilderment as his idealized dream of Daisy has outgrown the woman before him.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: A New York reporter arrives at Gatsby’s West Egg mansion one morning, mistakenly believing him to be a public figure, and is met with wild rumors—such as Gatsby living in a moving boat disguised as a house—spread by his guests; the narrative then reflects on Gatsby’s origins as James Gatz, a poor farm boy from North Dakota who, at seventeen, rowed out to Dan Cody’s yacht, the Tuolomee, on Lake Superior after encountering it, and spent five years aboard as a multipurpose attendant—serving as steward, jailor, and more—during travels across the continent, absorbing Cody’s lavish lifestyle and developing an aversion to alcohol; after Cody’s death, Ella Kaye boarded the yacht and prevented Gatsby from claiming his $25,000 inheritance, yet he retained the identity of Jay Gatsby, fully transformed. Weeks later, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon when Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit arrive on horseback; Gatsby, visibly nervous, offers drinks and hospitality, but Tom and Sloane are coldly dismissive, and when the woman invites Gatsby to supper, Sloane subtly blocks him, leaving him behind as they ride away. Later, Tom and Daisy attend one of Gatsby’s parties, where Daisy is unsettled by the excess and vulgarity of West Egg; Gatsby dances with her and later confides in Nick Carraway his belief that he can repeat the past, specifically reclaiming the moment five years earlier when he kissed Daisy under moonlight in Louisville, despite Nick Carraway’s warning that it is impossible, leaving Gatsby’s face tight and tired as the party ends in quiet despair.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On a sweltering summer afternoon, Nick Carraway arrives by train at the Buchanans' mansion to find Gatsby waiting; the house is eerily quiet after Gatsby replaced his original servants with untrustworthy ones linked to Wolfsheim. Inside, Daisy and Jordan lounge in the cool, dark salon while Tom argues on the telephone about a car sale. After luncheon, Daisy openly kisses Gatsby and declares her love, shocking Tom, who mocks Gatsby’s claim of Oxford education and accuses him of bootlegging through Wolfsheim’s drugstores. Tensions erupt as Daisy insists they go to town; Tom forces Gatsby to surrender his yellow coupé and takes control of it himself, driving off with Nick, Jordan, and Daisy toward New York, leaving Gatsby and Daisy behind. The group stops at Wilson’s garage in the Valley of Ashes, where Wilson—visibly ill and emotionally shattered—reveals he wants to leave with Myrtle and asks to buy Tom’s old car, while Myrtle watches from the window, mistaking Jordan for Tom’s wife and reacting with jealous terror. At the Plaza Hotel, the confrontation intensifies: Gatsby demands Daisy declare she never loved Tom; she reluctantly admits she never loved him but then breaks down, confessing she once loved both men. Tom triumphantly declares their marriage’s enduring truth and orders them to leave in Gatsby’s car. Later, Myrtle Wilson rushes out of the garage into the dusk and is struck and killed by a speeding yellow car that flees without stopping; Michaelis discovers her body with horrific injuries, and Wilson, now pale and trembling, stands dazed, repeating 'Oh, my Ga-od!' Tom and Nick arrive at the scene, where Tom denies driving the yellow car and claims he was in a blue coupé; he forcibly removes Wilson into the office and leaves with Nick, breaking down in tears as he calls the hit-and-run driver 'a God damned coward.' That night, Nick refuses to enter the Buchanans’ house and waits outside, where Gatsby confesses Daisy was driving the car that killed Myrtle and insists he will take the blame. Gatsby vows to wait all night to protect her, but Nick sees through the pantry window that Tom and Daisy are sitting together at the kitchen table, eating and speaking intimately, clearly reconciled. Nick leaves Gatsby standing alone in the moonlight, vigilantly watching over a house that no longer needs his protection.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: At dawn on Long Island, Nick Carraway rushes to Gatsby’s mansion after hearing a taxi arrive, finding Gatsby dejected as Daisy briefly appeared at her window before turning off the light. They search the dusty, unused rooms for cigarettes and smoke on the French windows, where Nick Carraway urges Gatsby to flee to Atlantic City or Montreal, but Gatsby refuses, clinging to the hope that Daisy will choose him; he then recounts his youth as a penniless officer who seduced Daisy under false pretenses of status, becoming irrevocably bound to her memory. In a later flashback, Gatsby reflects on the final afternoon before his departure for Oxford, sharing a silent, tender moment with Daisy in a fire-warmed room, where her reciprocated affection made him abandon his former ambitions. After returning from war, he traveled by day-coach to Louisville, revisiting places tied to Daisy and reaching desperately for the fading city as the train pulled away, realizing he lost the 'freshest and the best' part of that time. On the same day, Gatsby puts on his bathing suit, instructs the butler to bring calls to the pool, and carries a pneumatic mattress to the pool despite the open car’s broken fender being left unused; Nick Carraway, unable to leave, misses two trains and declares Gatsby worth more than 'the whole damn bunch put together,' receiving a radiant smile in return. Meanwhile, George Wilson, shattered by Myrtle’s death and fixated on the yellow car, finds a dog-leash in her bureau and believes its owner killed her; at dawn, he stares at the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg and declares 'God sees everything.' After wandering on foot to Port Roosevelt and Gad’s Hill, Wilson reappears in West Egg by half-past two, asking for Gatsby’s house. Later, gunshots are heard, and Nick Carraway arrives to find Gatsby’s body floating in the pool, with Wilson’s corpse discovered nearby in the grass, completing the tragedy.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: Following Gatsby’s death, Nick Carraway is left to manage the chaotic aftermath as police, photographers, and reporters swarm the mansion, while curious children slip through the yard; media narratives are shaped by a detective’s label of Wilson as a 'madman' and Catherine’s denial of any connection between Gatsby and Myrtle. Nick Carraway desperately tries to reach Daisy and Meyer Wolfsheim, receiving only silence or evasive responses, including a cryptic long-distance call from Chicago that ends abruptly when he announces Gatsby’s death. On the third day, Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives by train from Minnesota, visibly shaken and bundled in a cheap ulster, and is shown Gatsby’s body and a worn copy of Hopalong Cassidy containing his son’s childhood self-improvement schedule, revealing Gatsby’s disciplined ambition; most acquaintances refuse to attend the funeral—Klipspringer calls to request his tennis shoes, and Wolfsheim declines despite emotional distress, citing his rule against involvement after a death. The funeral proceeds at 3 p.m. with only Gatz, the Lutheran minister from Flushing, and servants present as rain falls; later, in a thick drizzle at the cemetery, the man with owl-eyed glasses—whom Nick Carraway had met months earlier in Gatsby’s library—appears unexpectedly, wipes rain from his glasses to view the grave, murmurs 'Amen to that' after a quote about the dead, and quietly calls Gatsby 'the poor son-of-a-bitch.' Nick Carraway then recalls vivid winter train journeys to the Midwest, defining his emotional connection to the homeland through sensory memories of street lamps, sleigh bells, and holly wreaths, reflecting that he, Gatsby, Daisy, Tom, and Jordan were all Westerners ill-suited to the East’s moral decay, symbolized by a haunting El Greco-like vision of West Egg. Before leaving, he meets Jordan Baker, who reveals she is engaged to another man; their conversation turns to their broken relationship and her accusation that he called her a bad driver, prompting him to admit he is thirty and too old to deceive himself about honor. In late October, he encounters Tom Buchanan on Fifth Avenue, who admits he told Wilson that Gatsby owned the car that killed Myrtle, justifying it by claiming Wilson was armed and dangerous, while emotionally framing his own grief over dog biscuits left at his flat; Nick shakes Tom’s hand, realizing Tom and Daisy are careless people who destroy lives and retreat into their wealth. Finally, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s empty house one last time at night, finding the lawn overgrown and an obscene word scrawled on the steps, which he erases with his shoe; walking to the beach, he reflects on Gatsby’s belief in the green light and the illusion of the future, concluding with the metaphor that we are borne back ceaselessly into the past.

plot_summary.plot_summary:
In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway moves from the Midwest to West Egg, Long Island, seeking opportunity in the bond business and renting a modest home beside the extravagant mansion of the mysterious Jay Gatsby. Through his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom—a wealthy, arrogant Yale alumnus with a violent temper and a mistress, Myrtle Wilson—Nick is drawn into the glittering yet morally hollow world of East Egg’s elite. He soon becomes entangled in Gatsby’s obsessive quest to reunite with Daisy, whom Gatsby had loved five years earlier as a young officer before being sent to war. Gatsby, who fabricated an aristocratic identity from humble origins as James Gatz, bought his mansion solely so Daisy could see the green light at the end of her dock, and he enlists Nick’s help to arrange a private meeting. Their reunion is emotionally charged but reveals the gap between Gatsby’s idealized vision of Daisy and the flawed woman before him.

As summer deepens, tensions rise between Gatsby and Tom, culminating in a volatile confrontation at the Plaza Hotel where Daisy, pressured by both men, admits she once loved both but cannot renounce her marriage. That afternoon, Myrtle Wilson is struck and killed by a speeding yellow car—Gatsby’s car—driven by Daisy, though Gatsby insists he will take the blame. George Wilson, Myrtle’s husband, consumed by grief and misled by Tom into believing Gatsby was both Myrtle’s lover and her killer, tracks Gatsby down. Meanwhile, Nick witnesses the moral collapse of those around him: Daisy and Tom retreat into their wealth after the tragedy, indifferent to the destruction they’ve caused; Gatsby’s so-called friends—including Meyer Wolfsheim and Klipspringer—vanish, refusing to attend his funeral; and Jordan Baker, whom Nick had grown close to, reveals her dishonesty and ends their relationship. Gatsby is shot dead by Wilson in his pool, and Wilson then takes his own life, leaving behind a silent, abandoned mansion.

Nick Carraway is left to organize Gatsby’s funeral, but nearly everyone who once flocked to his parties refuses to come, revealing the emptiness of the social world Gatsby tried so desperately to join. Only Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives, proudly displaying his son’s childhood self-improvement schedule, a testament to the disciplined dreamer beneath the facade. In the aftermath, Nick confronts Tom, who coldly admits he told Wilson about Gatsby’s car, justifying it as necessary protection. Disillusioned by the East’s moral decay and the careless cruelty of its inhabitants, Nick resolves to return home, reflecting on Gatsby’s unwavering belief in the future symbolized by the green light—how he reached for a dream that was always already behind him. The story ends with Nick’s haunting realization that humanity is perpetually borne back, ceaselessly, into the past.
